    organization principal, mirroring variables_patch_policy_test.go
    (BE-0114) and variables_put_policy_test.go (BE-0111) verbatim
    since env.write is the same action.
  - The Patch tests at this commit are wedged on the events[len-1]
    indexing bug. A future story should fix that pattern across
    organization_variable_patch_test.go; it is not on the BE-0115
    path.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - Hard-delete vs soft-delete: organization_variables is the first
    customer-facing resource in this codebase to take a HARD delete
    posture. The rule: a resource takes a soft delete (deletion_
    scheduled_at on organizations, revoked_at on api_keys) only when
    the row carries a continuing tie that must outlive the resource
    — typically an audit-log FK that must keep the row reachable, or
    a child cascade that must be ordered carefully. organization_
    variables has neither (the audit log records the deletion
    independently and there are no child tables), so the row is
    removed outright and the response carries the snapshot exactly
    as it stood at the moment of removal. A future resource that
    similarly has no continuing tie can follow this pattern — it is
    simpler than soft delete and gives the customer the same
    auditable record.
  - DELETE-on-a-named-resource response shape: a 200 OK carrying the
    pre-delete snapshot (mirroring api-key revoke and now this
    endpoint) is the right convention for a named-resource hard
    delete. An agent can confirm what was removed (id, key, version,
    timestamps) without a separate read. 204 No Content would have
    been less useful for an agent-friendly surface — there would be
    no way to confirm the resource id without re-listing.
  - Listing audit events in a test: ListByOrganization is ORDER BY
    occurred_at DESC, id DESC, so events[0] is NEWEST. A test that
    reads events[len-1] gets the OLDEST event, which in a fixture
    that issues seed-then-mutation is the seed event (with seed
    metadata), not the mutation under test. A test that probes the
    post-mutation state through ANOTHER mutation (e.g. a second
    Replace) files yet another audit event and pushes the mutation-
    under-test to events[1] — so the audit assertions must run
    BEFORE any further state-changing call, and post-state probes
    must read directly through the repository (not through another
    Replace).
  - Wire-side redaction chokepoint reuse: organizationVariableOf is
    the single projection function for GET, PUT (post-replace),
    PATCH, AND now DELETE — every variable endpoint that returns a
    variable on the wire flows through it, so the secret-to-sentinel
    contract holds uniformly. A future variable endpoint that needs
    a different projection (e.g. listing the audit history of a
    single variable) must NOT shadow this function; it should
    compose it or be obviously different in shape.

  - The variables CRUD authorization matrix is now fully pinned
    (BE-0108 read / BE-0111 PUT / BE-0114 PATCH / BE-0117 DELETE). All
    four use the same organizationIDResolver scoping the policy
    resource to the {org_id} path parameter at Kind=KindOrganization.
    PUT/PATCH/DELETE all require ActionEnvWrite (CapWrite); read
    requires ActionEnvRead (CapRead). The {key} sub-resource path is
    NEVER a deeper-scoped resource — it is a sub-resource within the
    organization-root scope — so scoped grants below the org root do
    not reach it.
  - Pattern for "{key} sub-resource on an org-root scope" matrix
    tests: identical structure to the bulk endpoint, with the URL
    {key} as a caller-submitted needle in deny-leak checks AND a
    distinct "data the orchestrator would have returned" fixture
    (different id/key/value from URL inputs and from sibling matrix
    fixtures) so a leak check searching for the seeded data never
    false-positives against unrelated fixtures or the URL needle.
  - For DELETE specifically: the deletion snapshot the deleter
    returns IS the response body — secret values must STILL redact
    to output.Sentinel on this path because a customer can never read
    a secret value back through DELETE either. The role-allow and
    grant-allow branches both need this assertion.
  - The deleter's input struct has only OrganizationID/Key/Actor*
    /Request*/Correlation* fields (no Value/IsSecret like PUT/PATCH),
    so the deny-path "deleter never reached" check is shorter than
    PATCH's — just OrganizationID == "" && Key == "".

- Learnings for future iterations:
  - The first endpoint of every resource layer is the one that adds the
    layer to NewHandler's parameter list — every test wrapper across
    httpapi/ needs a matching update. Two call-site shapes coexist:
    single-line `..., fakeAPIKeyRotator{}, nil)` (most files) and
    multi-line where the rotator is on one line and `nil)` is on the next
    (audit_events, limits, usage, variables). A single-line sed catches
    the first; the second needs either a multi-line awk/python pass or a
    manual visit. The 24-nil → 25-nil newRouteTable test stubs need a
    parallel update in 4-5 files. Plan both up front so the build doesn't
    bounce between vet errors.
  - The reader-port pattern carries verbatim for project listing:
    `httpapi.ProjectReader` interface declares the narrow contract;
    `*store.ProjectReader` adapts the repository inside Store.Read (never
    fresh SQL); the port is threaded NewHandler → newRouteTable → handler
    closure. fakeProjectReader{} (zero value returns empty slice) is the
    correct default for every other test wrapper because no other route
    consults it.
  - The testutil.Factory's slug() method suffixes every slug with the
    per-factory token (e.g., "alpha-999d270f…-4"). Tests asserting list
    ordering MUST keep the returned fixture's .Slug and assert against
    that value, never a hard-coded literal — the suffix is intentional
    so concurrent tests cannot collide.
  - For a list endpoint with a nil resolver (scope = principal home org),
    a grant-only principal is denied at the policy gate because the engine
    asks "does the grant scope CONTAIN the resource scope" — grant scope
    is narrower than the home-org resource scope, so it fails. This is
    the SAME behaviour as GET /v1/organizations (organizationsHandler)
    and is the correct enforcement: project-, environment-, and service-
    level grants do NOT imply project.read at the org-level scope. The
    policy matrix test for BE-0120 just needs to assert this deny path
    rather than implementing per-project filtering in the handler.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0120
- Added policy-matrix coverage for GET /v1/projects, proving action
  project.read cannot be bypassed by, or leak data because of, the
  principal's role, revoked credentials, home organization, or scoped
  grants. Mirrors the variables_policy_test.go shape one-for-one because
  project.read and env.read share the CapRead capability class — so the
  same role-allow matrix, revoked/expired (Disabled) denial, Support
  cross-tenant exception, and grant-containment chokepoints apply, and
  this file pins exactly the same engine clauses against project.read.
- File changed:
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_policy_test.go (new)
  - ralph/prd.json (BE-0120 passes=true)
  - ralph/progress.txt (this entry)
- The route uses a NIL ResourceResolver (routes.go), so RequireAuth
  authorizes against the principal's own home organization scope — there
  is NO path parameter that a foreign principal could fabricate to point
  the read at another tenant. The test file documents this structural
  difference vs. variables (which carries organizationIDResolver), and
  the wrong-organization principal test pins the cross-tenant boundary
  in two layers:
  1. Wire: an attacker in org_attacker hitting /v1/projects has the
     reader called with the attacker's home org id — never with a
     fabricated or caller-controlled value. The response body never
     echoes the victim's org id. This is the structural property that
     makes the endpoint cross-tenant-safe.
  2. Engine defence-in-depth: Decide(intruder, project.read,
     foreign_org_resource) -> ReasonDeniedCrossTenant; and
     Decide(support, project.read, foreign_org_resource) ->
     ReasonAllowedBySupport. These are engine-only pins today (no route
     constructs a foreign resource) so a future {org_id}-scoped project
     endpoint inherits a working cross-tenant deny + the support
     exception without re-deriving them.
- projects_policy_test.go covers:
  - TestListProjectsPolicyMatrixRoles: every built-in role
    (owner/admin/developer/viewer/ci/support) is allowed project.read
    via ReasonAllowedByRole (asserted at the engine level) and receives
    200 with the seeded two-project fixture in stable yalla.output.v1
    shape. Reader is reached with the principal's home org id, every
    column of the wire shape (project_id, organization_id, slug,
    display_name, version, created_at, updated_at) survives, and the
    fixture has two distinct versions (1, 2) so a future regression
    that hard-coded version=1 in the projection would fail here.
  - TestListProjectsPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys: a Disabled principal —
    even one whose underlying role is Owner — is rejected at the
    policy boundary with E_FORBIDDEN + ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled.
    Reader never runs; body never echoes the principal id, the org, or
    the seeded project ids/slugs/display names. Case names map 1:1 to
    the PRD principal classes ("revoked key", "expired key").
  - TestListProjectsPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal: the structural
    cross-tenant test described above. Wire-level: attacker sees only
    their own org via seenAttacker == ownOrg and body !~ victimOrg.
    Engine-level: ReasonDeniedCrossTenant for non-support owner of a
    foreign org, ReasonAllowedBySupport for Support of yalla on a
    foreign org. The Support engine clause is the same CapRead branch
    that fires for env.read / limits.read / usage.read.
  - TestListProjectsPolicyGrantContainment: all three PRD grant-
    containment properties pinned at the engine — sibling project
    (project grant does not reach proj_q via project.update),
    production environment (staging grant does not reach env_prod via
    environment.update), parent-level secrets (service grant does not
    reach env.write on the parent environment, and does not reach a
    sibling service). Tied back at the wire: the project-scoped key
    hitting /v1/projects at its OWN home org is 403 with
    ReasonDeniedOutOfScope (the scoped key cannot be widened to an
    organization-wide list — covers() is one-way), reader never reached,
    body does not leak the seeded project data. The org-level Viewer
    grant DOES cover the org-root scope (ReasonAllowedByGrant) and is
    allowed at the wire — this locks the CapRead requirement against
    the grant path so a future catalog change that upgraded project.read
    above CapRead would fail here (silently denying every org-level
    Viewer grantee) before it could regress a real customer. A final
    cross-tenant grant pin: the same project-grant carried by a
    principal whose home org is foreign is denied at the engine — a
    stolen scoped key cannot be smuggled across tenants by changing the
    principal's home org.
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -w internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_policy_test.go
  - go vet ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/...
  - go test -run 'TestListProjectsPolicy' ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/...
  - go test ./...
  - go test -race ./...
  - go vet ./...
- Results: all green. Initial wire-level cross-tenant assertion failed
  because the canonical fakeProjectReader (from projects_test.go)
  returns its seeded projects unconditionally regardless of the org id
  it was called with — so seeding it with the victim's projects caused
  them to surface in the attacker's 200 OK body. Fixed by seeding the
  attacker reader with the attacker's OWN projects and asserting
  structural isolation differently: the reader is hardcoded by the
  handler to use principal.OrganizationID (seenAttacker == ownOrg), and
  the response body never echoes the victim's org id literal. This is
  the correct way to assert the property against a non-content-keyed
  fake — the production ProjectReader.ListByOrganization tenant-scopes
  by definition, so the handler-side contract under test is which org
  id the handler asks for, not what the fake returns.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - The CapRead role matrix here is identical to env.read / limits.read
    / usage.read in shape but with different fixtures. A future
    refactor could lift the matrix into a shared table-driven helper
    parameterised on (action, fixture, decoder) so a new CapRead
    endpoint can adopt the matrix in five lines; intentionally not
    done in this story to keep the change focused.
  - BE-0123 (POST /v1/projects policy matrix) is priority 1 but
    depends on BE-0121 (POST /v1/projects implement) — which is
    priority 2 and not yet implemented. The next iteration should
    pick BE-0121 to unblock BE-0122 (contract tests) + BE-0123
    (policy matrix). The shape of BE-0123 will diverge from this
    file: project.create is CapWrite (not CapRead), so the role
    matrix splits along the write capability class (viewer denies,
    Support denies cross-tenant), and the grant containment test
    must prove an organization-level Viewer grant is DENIED
    project.create (because the action requires CapWrite, which
    Viewer does not hold) — the inverse of the CapRead-allowed
    assertion in this file.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - For nil-resolver list endpoints (organization-root scope of the
    principal's home org), the cross-tenant property is STRUCTURAL —
    there is no path parameter to forge. The policy matrix test still
    needs to pin (a) that the reader is hardcoded to the principal's
    home org id and (b) the engine-level cross-tenant verdict
    defence-in-depth, so a future {org_id}-scoped variant inherits a
    working cross-tenant deny. Do not try to assert a wire-level 403
    for a wrong-organization principal on a nil-resolver route — the
    route returns 200 with the principal's own org's projects, which
    is correct.
  - When asserting tenant isolation against a fake reader that returns
    its seeded fixture unconditionally (the canonical pattern in
    projects_test.go and variables_test.go for keyed-by-orgID fakes
    that only echo the call's org id), do not seed the fake with the
    victim's data — that data WILL surface in the body because the
    fake does not enforce the production tenant-scope. Instead seed
    with the principal's OWN org's data and prove (i) the reader was
    called with the right org id (seenSomething == expectedOrg) and
    (ii) the body does not echo the victim's org id literal. The
    production ProjectReader.ListByOrganization is tenant-scoped at
    the SQL layer; the handler-side contract under test is which org
    id the handler asks for, not what the fake returns.
  - The engine's same-tenant role-cap check fires BEFORE the
    cross-tenant Support exception, so a Support principal reading its
    OWN organization is allowed via ReasonAllowedByRole — NOT
    ReasonAllowedBySupport. The Support exception only applies when
    principal.OrganizationID != resource.Scope.OrganizationID. This
    matters for the matrix-roles test (which asserts
    ReasonAllowedByRole for support same-tenant) and for the
    wrong-organization test (which asserts ReasonAllowedBySupport for
    support cross-tenant). Asserting ReasonAllowedBySupport for support
    same-tenant would silently fail.
  - Mirror an existing policy matrix file exactly when adding the next
    one — variables_policy_test.go is the canonical CapRead matrix
    shape, projects_policy_test.go is now the canonical CapRead matrix
    shape for nil-resolver list endpoints. Future CapRead nil-resolver
    list endpoints (members, api-keys, etc.) should be derived from
    projects_policy_test.go's structure; future CapRead resolver-bound
    endpoints (variables, limits, usage) from variables_policy_test.go.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0121
- What was implemented: POST /v1/projects, the create-project endpoint —
  the second customer-facing mutating endpoint in Yalla's
  Organization -> Project -> Environment -> Service hierarchy, and the
  unblock for BE-0122 (contract tests) + BE-0123 (policy matrix, priority 1).
  - internal/controlplane/store/projectservice.go: extended ProjectService
    to take an AuditAppender dependency and to file an immutable audit
    record inside the same transaction as the desired-state write. The
    fixed-order unit of work is now: authorize, reserve quota, INSERT
    project row, enqueue provisioning job, append audit. Every failure
    after validation rolls the whole transaction back, so a created
    project can never exist without its job AND audit trail. Added
    Actor*/Request*/Correlation* fields to CreateProjectInput so the
    httpapi handler can pass the resolved principal and request
    correlation through. NewProjectService rejects a nil audit appender at
    construction.

    success test to assert the audit row commits with the right
    action/actor/correlation/metadata; added
    TestProjectServiceCreateRequiresActorOrg covering the wiring guard

    store.NewAuditRepository() through every existing NewProjectService
    call; added Actor*/correlation fields to the shared newCreateInput
    fixture; added listProjectAuditEvents helper mirroring the
    organizationservice_test.go pattern.
  - internal/controlplane/store/internal_test.go: added nopAuditAppender
    and extended TestNewProjectServiceRejectsNilDependencies to cover the
    new nil-audit guard.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects.go: added the ProjectCreator
    port, createProjectRequest/createProjectPayload DTOs,

    decode (strict, unknown-field rejected), read principal off context,
    forward to ProjectCreator with the principal's home org as both
    OrganizationID (the create target) and ActorOrgID (the audit tenant).
    A nil principal or nil creator surfaces as Internal; a missing creator

  - ralph/prd.json, ralph/progress.txt
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -w .
  - go mod tidy
  - go vet ./...
  - go test ./...
  - go test -race ./...
- Results: all green. goimports is not installed on this machine; gofmt
  and go vet are both clean.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - BE-0123 (priority 1, POST /v1/projects policy matrix) is now
    unblocked. The matrix shape diverges from BE-0120's nil-resolver list
    matrix: project.create is CapWrite, so the role matrix splits along
    the write capability class — viewer denies (the inverse of BE-0120's
    viewer-allows assertion), support denies even same-tenant, and a
    grant-only principal whose grants do not contain the home org denies.
    The principal classes the PRD names are owner/admin/developer/viewer/
    ci/support + revoked/expired keys + wrong-organization principal.
  - BE-0122 (contract tests) and BE-0123 (policy matrix) can be picked
    in either order; the contract tests are easier and the policy matrix
    benefits from the contract tests' fixtures.
  - The Authorizer/QuotaReserver/JobEnqueuer placeholders in main.go are
    correct-but-empty — they need real adapters when (a) the project
    quota plan resolver story lands and (b) the provisioning worker
    story lands. The HTTP RequireAuth middleware is the authoritative
    gate today; production traffic cannot bypass the policy.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - When extending a unit-of-work service to record an audit event, add
    Actor{ID,Kind,OrgID} + RequestID/CorrelationID fields to the input
    struct; the httpapi handler fills them from
    policy.PrincipalFromContext + telemetry.FromContext. The audit row's
    OrganizationID is the actor's home org (the tenant the audit log
    lives under), while ResourceID is the resource being created. Reject
    a blank ActorOrgID as Internal — it is a wiring error, never a
    client error — before opening the transaction.
  - Existing test files with NewHandler call sites all share one
    signature, but a small minority pass named parameter variables (e.g.
    "reader" instead of "fakeProjectReader{}") in the last positional
    slot. A regex pass on literal "fakeProjectReader{}" handles 35/36
    sites; the holdout (listProjectsHandlerFor) needs a manual patch.
    Future additions to NewHandler's signature will face the same
    pattern.
  - The route table arity is now 26 (build + 25 readers/services). New
    newRouteTable test sites in newly-added test files must use 25 nils
    after BuildInfo{}. A one-line audit (counting nils in the source) is
    the fastest way to verify.
  - The strict JSON decoder (validate.DecodeJSON with disallowUnknownFields)
    is the load-bearing piece of structural tenant isolation for POST
    endpoints: the request body has no organization_id field, and a body
    that smuggles one is rejected as a 400 before the handler even reads
    the principal. The handler builds CreateProjectInput.OrganizationID
    from p.OrganizationID, never from the body, so a caller cannot point
    the write at another tenant even if the decoder were to accept the
    field. Both layers are required — defense-in-depth.
  - Placeholder Authorizer/Quota/Jobs adapters in main.go are correct as
    long as they are: (a) explicitly typed and named with a TODO-bearing
    comment, (b) constructed at startup so store.NewProjectService's nil
    guards still fire on a misconfigured binary, (c) never silently
    zero-valued (a nil dependency must remain a startup error). The
    pattern matches the way runtime.NewMeta is wired before the real
    migration probe lands.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0123
- What was implemented: policy matrix coverage for POST /v1/projects,
  the second policy-matrix file in the project family (after BE-0120's
  project.read matrix), and the first CapWrite matrix on a nil-resolver
  route (every prior CapWrite matrix — variables put/patch/delete —
  uses organizationIDResolver). project.create is CapWrite, so the
  matrix splits along the write capability class: Owner/Admin/Developer
  allow in own org (ReasonAllowedByRole); Viewer/CI/Support deny in own
  org (ReasonDeniedNoCapability); EVERY role denies cross-tenant
  (ReasonDeniedCrossTenant — CapWrite is outside the engine's support
  cross-tenant exception, unlike CapRead). Privileged Yalla support
  that needs to create a project on a customer's behalf goes through
  explicit break-glass admin tooling, never this customer-facing route.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_create_policy_test.go (new):
    four tests drive the real NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine() —
    the production request path — so a regression in the middleware,
    the action catalog, or the engine fails here. The file adds two
    small fixtures (canonicalCreateProjectInput, canonicalCreatedProject)
    and one deny-leak guard (createProjectDenyBodyLeak) and otherwise
    consumes the shared scaffolding from projects_create_test.go
    (createProjectHandlerFor, postProjects, createProjectRequestBody,
    decodeCreateProject, decodeCreateProjectError, fakeProjectCreator)
    and the wider httpapi test fixtures (orgPrincipal, decodeError).
  - TestCreateProjectPolicyMatrixRoles is the role matrix proper. It
    runs every built-in role (owner/admin/developer/viewer/ci/support)
    through the full request path. Allow rows pin: 201 yalla.output.v1,
    creator reached with input.OrganizationID == principal home org,
    input.ActorOrgID == principal home org, input.ActorID == principal
    id (so the audit row names the actor verbatim), and the canned
    created project echoed back. Deny rows pin: 403 yalla.error.v1,
    error message contains the stable reason, creator MUST NOT run
    (gotInput.OrganizationID and gotInput.ActorID both unset), and the
    body never echoes any of the recognisable request-body or canned-
    project fields. Both the engine verdict and the wire verdict are
    asserted side by side so a future drift between the two fails here.
  - TestCreateProjectPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys covers the two PRD-
    named credential-disabled cases ("revoked key", "expired key").
    Both surface to the policy engine as Disabled=true; underlying role
    is Owner so a working credential WOULD allow it, ensuring Disabled
    is load-bearing. Asserts: 403, ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled in the
    message, creator never reached, body never echoes the principal id,
    the org id, or the request data.
  - TestCreateProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal pins the cross-
    tenant boundary. The route uses a nil resolver and the strict JSON
    decoder rejects organization_id in the body, so the wire surface
    offers no path for a foreign principal to point the write at
    another tenant — tenant isolation is structural and the creator is
    ALWAYS called with the principal's home org id. The wire half
    proves an attacker still creates in its OWN org and that the
    response body never echoes the victim's org id. The engine half is
    a sub-test loop (cross_tenant_owner/admin/developer/viewer/ci/
    support) authorizing project.create against a foreign org Resource;
    every role — INCLUDING Support — denies via
    ReasonDeniedCrossTenant, because CapWrite is outside the engine's
    `CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)` exception. This is the
    load-bearing distinction from BE-0120 (project.read), where the
    same Support cross-tenant probe is the documented ALLOW exception.
  - TestCreateProjectPolicyGrantContainment pins the three PRD-named
    grant-containment properties (sibling project, production
    environment, parent-level secrets) at the engine via project/env/
    service-scoped admin grants, then ties the property back to the
    wire by proving a project-scoped grantee is denied POST /v1/projects
    at its own home org with ReasonDeniedOutOfScope (creator never
    runs, body never echoes request data). The matrix additionally
    pins: (a) org-level VIEWER grant denies via
    ReasonDeniedNoCapability — the load-bearing distinction from
    BE-0120's project.read containment where an org-level Viewer grant
    is sufficient; (b) org-level DEVELOPER grant allows via
    ReasonAllowedByGrant, with the wire returning 201, the creator
    reached on the principal's home org id, and the actor id being the
    grantee's id verbatim; (c) a project-scoped grant whose carrier
    principal is planted in a foreign org denies — stealing a key
    cannot smuggle a write across tenants.
- Files changed:
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_create_policy_test.go (new)
  - ralph/prd.json, ralph/progress.txt
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -w .
  - go mod tidy
  - go vet ./...
  - go test ./...
  - go test -race ./...
- Results: all green. goimports is not installed on this machine; gofmt
  and go vet are both clean. The new file is the only addition; no
  existing file changed.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - Next failing project-family stories: BE-0124 (implement GET
    /v1/projects/{project_id}) and BE-0126 (its policy matrix). The
    matrix shape will diverge again — GET /v1/projects/{project_id}
    will use a project-id resolver (not the nil resolver and not the
    org-id resolver), so the scoped-grant containment property
    inverts: a project-scoped Admin grant for THAT project is the
    allow path, while an org-scoped Viewer grant is the role-allowed
    path. The cross-tenant deny will be a 404 (path id not found in
    the principal's home org) rather than a 403 cross-tenant, since
    the resolver would not surface a foreign-org id.
  - The route description string in routes.go for POST /v1/projects
    asserts "owner, admin, developer, ci" as the admitted role set,
    but the actual policy engine denies CI (CI's capset is
    CapSelf+CapRead+CapDeploy, no CapWrite). The matrix here pins the
    engine's truth (CI denied). A future BE-0XXX could correct the
    description to "owner, admin, developer" so the OpenAPI document
    stops misleading agents reading the discovery surface; the matrix
    will catch the wire/catalog half of any such drift.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The CapWrite-on-nil-resolver matrix shape is structurally NEW in
    this codebase. Prior CapWrite matrices (variables put/patch/delete,
    organization patch) all use organizationIDResolver, so they prove
    "cross-tenant {org_id} denies as 403" at the WIRE. The project.create
    matrix proves the same property STRUCTURALLY: the wire offers no
    foreign-org path at all, so the only place the cross-tenant
    boundary can fail is the engine. The matrix therefore drops the
    wire-cross-tenant test and replaces it with a sub-test loop that
    walks every role through the engine's foreign-org Resource probe.
    Future CapWrite-on-nil-resolver endpoints (none yet planned, but
    BE-0103-style CapAdmin-on-nil-resolver may appear) can copy this
    shape verbatim.
  - The CapWrite-vs-CapRead policy distinction at the grant boundary
    is load-bearing: an org-level Viewer grant SATISFIES the scope
    requirement for project.create (covers() the org root) but FAILS
    the capability requirement (Viewer's capset doesn't include
    CapWrite). The engine reports this as ReasonDeniedNoCapability,
    not ReasonDeniedOutOfScope — distinguishing it from the project-
    scoped grant denial. Both denies are asserted in the matrix so a
    future engine regression that conflated the two reasons would
    fail here. The sister allow assertion — that an org-level
    Developer grant IS sufficient — locks the CapWrite requirement
    against the grant path: a future catalog change that downgraded
    project.create to CapRead would silently allow every org-level
    Viewer grantee to create projects, and the deny assertion here
    would fail before it could regress a customer.
  - The strict JSON decoder is doing structural work in the
    wrong-organization test: a foreign org id smuggled into the body
    is rejected as 400 (unknown field), so a non-attacker test (which
    posts a clean body) STILL never receives a path to point the
    write at another tenant. The matrix doesn't need a separate
    "body-injection cross-tenant" case because the contract suite
    (TestCreateProjectIgnoresOrganizationIDInBody) already pins that
    decoder behaviour. Cross-tenant on a nil-resolver POST is
    therefore the engine's job, not the wire's; the matrix probes
    the engine directly.
  - A deny-path leak guard for a CREATE endpoint needles for the
    REQUEST-body fields (caller-supplied) AND the canned-creator-
    output fields (server-side). Both are recognisable on purpose
    (prj_matrix_alpha / matrix-alpha / Matrix Alpha). A denied
    response that accidentally rendered request fields would mean the
    handler echoed user input after policy denial (a tenant boundary
    smell); a denied response that accidentally rendered creator
    output would mean the creator ran and the response leaked even
    though the wire said 403. Two needles, two different regressions
    — keeping them in one guard means a future leak in either
    direction fails the same assertion.
  - Subtest-loop pattern for engine-only probes inside a primarily-
    wire test: TestCreateProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal
    opens with one wire probe (own-tenant 201) and then nests t.Run
    sub-tests for the cross-tenant engine probes per role. Each
    sub-test is t.Parallel() (each closes over its own tc shadow);
    the parent test is also t.Parallel() at the file level. Mixing
    one wire setup with a per-role engine sub-test loop keeps the
    test name surface useful (cross_tenant_owner/cross_tenant_admin/
    ...) and lets a failing role show up by name in test output.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0124 - Implement GET /v1/projects/{project_id}
- Added the third project-family endpoint: GET /v1/projects/{project_id}.
  Route is wired through the existing newRouteTable single source of truth,
  registered after POST /v1/projects so OpenAPI lists list/create/get
  contiguously. Action: project.read (CapRead). Resolver:
  projectIDResolver — derives the policy.Resource from the principal's
  home organization id (read from the request context the auth
  middleware attached before the resolver runs) plus the {project_id}
  path parameter. The resolver never trusts a caller-supplied org id;
  cross-tenant project ids reach the tenant-scoped repository query
  with the principal's home org id and are reported as a deterministic
  404 by the persistence layer, never revealing another tenant's data.
- Persistence layer: extended *store.ProjectReader with GetProject(ctx,
  organizationID, projectID) (Project, error), opening a short-lived
  read-only transaction and delegating to the existing
  ProjectRepository.Get — which already does tenant-scoped filtering
  by (organization_id, id) and maps pgx.ErrNoRows to apierr.NotFound.
  Added a new integration test TestProjectReaderGetProject proving:
  (a) the owner of a project gets the row, (b) a cross-tenant id is
  reported as NotFound (E_NOT_FOUND), and (c) an unknown id is
  reported as NotFound. Validated against an isolated migrated
  Postgres via docker-compose postgres + YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL.
- HTTP layer: extended the ProjectReader interface in httpapi with
  GetProject (the list-and-get reader is now a single port, mirroring
  the OrganizationReader pattern). Added getProjectHandler,
  getProjectPayload, and projectIDResolver in projects.go. Extended
  the fakeProjectReader in projects_test.go with project/getErr/
  gotGetOrgID/gotGetProjectID fields so the new handler tests can
  assert which (org, project) pair was forwarded to the store
  without re-implementing the fake.
- Unit tests (new file projects_get_test.go, 11 tests):
  - TestGetProjectReturnsRequestedProject — happy path, full envelope
    shape, every wire field projected from the store row.
  - TestGetProjectForwardsHomeOrganizationAndPathID — proves the
    reader is called with principal.OrganizationID + path
    project_id, never with caller-controlled input.
  - TestGetProjectReturnsNotFoundForUnknownProject — typed 404
    E_NOT_FOUND.
  - TestGetProjectCrossTenantIDBehavesAsNotFound — cross-tenant id
    surfaces as 404 (not 403, not 200), and the response body does
    not echo the foreign organization id.
  - TestGetProjectRequiresBearerToken — 401 E_AUTH; reader sentinel
    proves the handler never ran.
  - TestGetProjectRejectsInvalidCredential — 401 E_AUTH on
    auth.ErrInvalidCredentials.
  - TestGetProjectRejectsDisabledPrincipal — 403 E_FORBIDDEN at the
    policy engine; reader never ran.
  - TestGetProjectAllowsOrganizationWideViewer — Viewer (the
    lowest CapRead-bearing role) is sufficient.
  - TestGetProjectRejectsGrantOnlyKeyForSiblingProject — a grant for
    prj_alpha cannot read prj_beta (containment is one-way).
  - TestGetProjectAllowsGrantOnlyKeyForTargetProject — a grant for
    prj_alpha can read prj_alpha (covers itself).
  - TestGetProjectPropagatesDependencyFailure — store outage is 5xx,
    never collapsed to 404; raw driver text never leaks.

- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - BE-0125 (contract tests for GET /v1/projects/{project_id}) and
    BE-0126 (policy matrix coverage for GET /v1/projects/{project_id})
    are the next failing project-family stories. BE-0125 will
    consolidate envelope-shape, request-id propagation, and the
    OpenAPI operation-registration assertions into a contract suite;
    much of what it requires already ships in projects_get_test.go.
    BE-0126 will add the deeper policy matrix (owner/admin/developer/
    viewer/ci/support, revoked key, expired key, wrong-org principal)
    against the new projectIDResolver scope shape — the containment
    inversion noted in the BE-0123 follow-up: a project-scoped Admin
    grant for THAT project is the load-bearing happy path, where the
    list endpoint's matrix required an organization-level grant.
  - PATCH /v1/projects/{project_id} (BE-0127) can reuse projectIDResolver
    as-is; the store layer already has ProjectRepository.UpdateDisplayName
    with the If-Match optimistic-concurrency contract wired and
    integration-tested.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Resolver pattern for project-id and deeper-scoped endpoints:
    *do NOT* try to read the project's organization from the database
    inside the resolver — keep the resolver pure path+context. The
    correct trick is to pull the principal's home OrganizationID from
    the request context the auth middleware attached BEFORE the
    resolver runs (policy.PrincipalFromContext(r.Context()) — yes,
    the ResourceResolver signature is func(r *http.Request)
    policy.Resource but the context already carries the principal).
    Then the resolver returns Scope{OrganizationID: principal.HomeOrg,
    ProjectID: r.PathValue("project_id")}. Cross-tenant attempts are
    absorbed by the tenant-scoped repository query (404), not by the
    policy engine (which sees the principal's own org). This is the
    same shape PATCH/DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id} should adopt;
    keep the test "TestGetProjectCrossTenantIDBehavesAsNotFound" as
    the canonical regression check that this stays true.
  - The store reader-adapter pattern is now codified for project:
    *Reader composes *Repository, never issues its own SQL, opens a
    short-lived read tx per call via Store.Read. New methods on the
    reader should be a thin transactional wrapper around an existing
    Querier-accepting repository method so the tenant-scoping
    guarantees proved in the repository's integration tests are
    inherited for free. Mirrors OrganizationReader.GetOrganization
    and ProjectReader.ListProjects exactly.
  - When extending an httpapi port interface that fakes already
    satisfy in test files, prefer extending the fake in-place over
    duplicating it. The fakeProjectReader now carries both List and
    Get state (projects/err/gotOrgID for list, project/getErr/
    gotGetOrgID/gotGetProjectID for get); the zero value still works
    everywhere the public-surface and unrelated route suites used
    it, so no cross-test churn was needed.
  - auth.ErrInvalidCredentials (plural; not ErrInvalidCredential).
    The middleware writeAuthError matches by errors.Is on the
    pluralised sentinel; tests for endpoints that exercise the
    invalid-credential path should use the same name.
  - For dependency-failure tests, the message-redaction assertion
    (substring check on raw driver text like "connection refused")
    catches accidental leakage cheaply and is a good pattern to
    propagate to every new endpoint test suite. It complements the
    typed-status check rather than replacing it.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0126 - Add policy matrix coverage for GET /v1/projects/{project_id}
- What was implemented: policy-matrix coverage for the deep-resource read
  endpoint GET /v1/projects/{project_id}. Where projects_get_test.go pins
  the wire contract (BE-0124), the new file
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_get_policy_test.go pins the
  authorization contract: that action project.read cannot be bypassed by —
  or leak data because of — the principal's role, revoked credentials,
  home organization, or scoped grants. Four tests, all running through
  the real NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine() (production request
  path):
    * TestGetProjectPolicyMatrixRoles — every built-in role drives the
      route in its own org. All six roles hold CapRead, so the matrix is
      "all allow"; each subtest pins the engine reason
      (ReasonAllowedByRole), proves the reader is called with the
      principal's home org id AND the {project_id} path parameter, and
      asserts the response carries the canonical project's full
      projectResource.
    * TestGetProjectPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys — Disabled principal
      whose underlying role would have allowed it: 403 carries
      ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled, the reader never runs, and the
      denied body never echoes the principal id, the organization id,
      or the canonical project's identifiers.
    * TestGetProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal — wire-level AND
      engine-level cross-tenant. Wire: a foreign project_id reaches the
      reader with the attacker's home org id (the resolver pins
      Scope.OrganizationID to principal.OrganizationID, never the
      caller) and the tenant-scoped store returns NotFound — surfacing
      as a deterministic 404, never 200 with foreign data and never 403
      that would confirm existence. Body must not echo the foreign org
      id. Engine: pins ReasonDeniedCrossTenant for every non-support
      role and ReasonAllowedBySupport for Support (CapRead is INSIDE
      the engine's cross-tenant exception), as defence-in-depth for a
      future endpoint that constructs a resource with a foreign-org
      scope.
    * TestGetProjectPolicyGrantContainment — scoped grants. Engine: a
      project-level Admin grant naming THIS project allows project.read
      (ReasonAllowedByGrant), but a SIBLING project denies via
      ReasonDeniedOutOfScope; an env-level grant denies project.read on
      the parent project (covers() is one-way); a service-level grant
      denies project.read on the parent project AND env.write on the
      parent environment AND service.update on a sibling service; an
      org-level Viewer grant allows project.read on any project
      (Viewer holds CapRead, ReasonAllowedByGrant). Wire ties: the
      project grantee on the target project receives the project; the
      same grantee on a sibling project, an env-scoped grantee on the
      parent project, and a service-scoped grantee on the parent
      project all 403 with the stable out-of-scope reason, the reader
      never runs, and the canonical project's id/slug/display name
      never appear in the body. The org-level Viewer grantee is
      end-to-end allowed at the wire.
- Files changed:
    * internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_get_policy_test.go (new,
      pure test file, no production code).
    * ralph/prd.json — flipped BE-0126.passes from false to true.
    * ralph/progress.txt — this entry.
- Verification run: gofmt -w ., go mod tidy (no diff), go vet ./...,
  go test ./..., go test -race ./.... All passed. goimports not
  installed (documented as a no-op).
- Results: 0 failures, every existing test still passes. The new file
  drives the real NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine() so a regression
  in the action catalog, the projectIDResolver, builtinRoleCaps, the
  engine's cross-tenant or grant clauses, or the wire-renderer fails
  here.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups: none for this story. BE-0127 (PATCH
  /v1/projects/{project_id}), BE-0128 (DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id}),
  and similar deep-resource policy matrices are next; they can copy
  this file's shape verbatim because the resolver scope is identical —
  swap project.read for the relevant CapWrite/CapAdmin action and
  re-derive the role allow/deny split from defaultActionCatalog (a
  CapWrite policy matrix on a project-level resource would look like
  this file with Viewer/CI/Support denying via ReasonDeniedNoCapability
  and Support's cross-tenant exception withdrawn, mirroring the
  CapWrite-on-nil-resolver shape in projects_create_policy_test.go but
  on a deeper resource).
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - The "deep-resource resolver" policy matrix (project_id, future
    environment_id, service_id) is the third distinct shape after
    nil-resolver (POST /v1/projects, projects_create_policy_test.go)
    and organizationIDResolver (env.write/env.read on {org_id}). The
    key load-bearing distinction is that the resource scope is built
    from BOTH the principal's home org AND the path id — so the
    cross-tenant clause CANNOT fire on the wire (same-tenant by
    construction), and tenant-isolation for a foreign path id is
    enforced at the PERSISTENCE layer as a 404, not at the policy
    boundary as a 403. The test must pin both: the wire 404 with no
    foreign-tenant body echo, and the engine 403/allow defence-in-depth
    for a hypothetical foreign-scope resource. Both are necessary
    because the wire surface can never reach the engine's cross-tenant
    clause through this endpoint, but a future admin-tool variant
    might.
  - A project-level resource is "reachable" from an org-level grant
    (org scope covers everything in it) AND from a project-level grant
    naming THIS project. It is NOT reachable from env- or
    service-level grants (covers() is one-way). The grant matrix at
    this depth therefore has a richer allow-by-grant row than the
    nil-resolver matrix (where ONLY an org-level grant could ever
    cover the org root): a project-level Admin grant allows, an
    org-level Viewer grant allows (both via ReasonAllowedByGrant),
    while env-/service-/sibling-project grants all deny via
    ReasonDeniedOutOfScope. The wire suite must exercise the
    target-project allow row alongside the sibling-project deny —
    they're different engine paths even though the principal and the
    handler look identical.
  - The fakeProjectReader was already extended for GET by BE-0124
    (project / getErr / gotGetOrgID / gotGetProjectID). No fake-fixture
    extension was needed for this story — the existing leak-guard
    pattern (canonical canonical*Project + *DenyBodyLeak) carries
    cleanly. Future deep-resource matrices that reuse a multi-route
    fake should adopt the same convention: keep capture pointers
    distinct per route (got*OrgID, got*ProjectID, got*EnvID,
    got*ServiceID) so a single fake satisfies multiple route ports
    without leaking state between them.
  - listProjectsHandlerFor wires both the list AND get routes (it
    builds the full NewHandler stack with the same ProjectReader). The
    helper name has historic baggage from when only the list route
    existed; the get-route policy tests reuse it as-is rather than
    introducing a "projectsHandlerFor" sibling, matching the pattern
    BE-0124 established. A future cosmetic rename should sweep both
    suites at once.
  - Variable named projectResource shadows the unexported
    projectResource struct from projects.go inside the test function
    scope. This is legal Go and harmless here (the test never refers
    to the type by name in that function — it accesses fields through
    env.Data.Project), but it's a smell worth avoiding in future
    suites. Prefer a non-colliding local name like
    `projectScopeResource` or `targetResource` in new files.
  - apierr.NotFound(kind, id) is the canonical way to make a fake
    persistence port return a typed 404. It maps to E_NOT_FOUND
    through the apierr -> apienvelope plumbing; tests should decode
    against that code, and assert the foreign tenant's org id does
    not appear in env.Error.Message (the persistence layer must
    redact foreign identity even when the request body is empty).

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0129
- What was implemented: policy-matrix coverage for PATCH
  /v1/projects/{project_id} — the authorization contract of the
  endpoint BE-0127 wires, parallel to BE-0123 for POST and BE-0126
  for GET /v1/projects/{project_id}.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_update_policy_test.go (new):
    one canonical fixture (canonicalUpdateProject / canonicalPatchBody
    / canonicalPatchDisplayName) + a single leak guard
    (updateProjectDenyBodyLeak) used by every deny branch, then four
    tests that drive the REAL NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine()
    against fake Authenticator + fake ProjectUpdater (the production
    request path minus the database):
    - TestUpdateProjectPolicyMatrixRoles tables all six built-in
      roles against project.update at a same-tenant project resource.
      CapWrite splits the matrix: Owner / Admin / Developer allow via
      ReasonAllowedByRole (200 + updater reached with home_org + path
      project_id + actor id + decoded display_name patch); Viewer /
      CI / Support deny via ReasonDeniedNoCapability (403 + updater
      never reached + body never echoes the canonical row or the
      caller-supplied patch). CI denies despite holding CapDeploy —
      CapDeploy is service lifecycle, not desired-state mutation.
    - TestUpdateProjectPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys proves a Disabled
      Owner principal (revoked OR expired credential) is denied via
      ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled, the updater never runs, and the
      body never echoes the principal id, the organization id, the
      path-supplied project id, or the canonical row / patch body.
    - TestUpdateProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal pins the
      cross-tenant boundary at TWO layers: at the wire, an attacker
      in org_attacker patching prj_victim_alpha reaches the fake
      updater with the principal's HOME org id (never a foreign id),
      the production-shape NotFound surfaces as 404 E_NOT_FOUND, and
      the response body never echoes org_victim even though no wire
      input could place it there; at the engine, EVERY built-in
      role (including Support) is denied via ReasonDeniedCrossTenant
      against a foreign-org Resource — CapWrite is OUTSIDE the
      engine's cross-tenant CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)
      exception, which is the load-bearing distinction from
      project.read's matrix (read admits Support cross-tenant via
      ReasonAllowedBySupport, update does not).
    - TestUpdateProjectPolicyGrantContainment proves scoped-grant
      containment for project.update across five wire tie-ins:
      project-Admin grant on TARGET project allows (200, updater
      reached with the principal id verbatim); project-Admin grant
      on SIBLING project denies via ReasonDeniedOutOfScope (403,
      updater never reached, no leak); project-VIEWER grant on the
      same project denies via ReasonDeniedNoCapability (the new
      assertion vs project.read — viewer covers the resource but
      does not hold the write capability); env-scoped grant on the
      parent project denies via ReasonDeniedOutOfScope (covers() is
      one-way — deeper scope cannot reach shallower resource);
      service-scoped grant on the parent project denies the same
      way; org-level Admin grant on the same resource is allowed via
      ReasonAllowedByGrant end-to-end; org-level Viewer grant on the
      same resource denies via ReasonDeniedNoCapability (the
      mirror-image of the org-level Viewer ALLOW on project.read).
    - And the engine-twin of the wrong-org wire property is pinned
      against a project-scoped admin key planted in a foreign home
      org: the cross-tenant guard fires before the grant is even
      considered, so a stolen scoped key cannot be smuggled across
      tenants.

  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_update_policy_test.go (new)
  - ralph/prd.json (BE-0129 passes -> true)
  - ralph/progress.txt (append)

  - go test -run TestUpdateProjectPolicy ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/...

  govulncheck still not installed locally (documented in earlier
  iterations).
- Remaining risks / follow-ups:
  - The next p=1 unfinished story is BE-0132 (policy matrix coverage
    for DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id}), which is blocked on
    BE-0130 (implement DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id}) and BE-0131
    (contract tests). DELETE on projects must follow the
    soft-delete-via-deletion_scheduled_at pattern already pinned for
    organizations (Codebase Patterns), so the next iteration should
    extend the schema/repository the same way before policy-matrix
    coverage lands.
  - Routes.go currently states that project.update admits "owner,
    admin, developer, ci" (route description block for PATCH
    /v1/projects/{project_id}), which is stale wording — CI holds
    CapDeploy, not CapWrite, and the engine denies it. This was the
    one drive-by I caught while writing the matrix; not fixed here
    because routes.go descriptions are also OpenAPI-surfaced and a
    description-only change is its own micro-story. A future BE story
    that updates the OpenAPI/route description should sync the CI
    wording with the actual catalog mapping.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - For a CapWrite endpoint's policy matrix, the structure is a
    cross product of three axes: (a) role -> capability, (b) scope
    containment, (c) cross-tenant clause inclusion. The CapWrite
    surface differs from CapRead in TWO axes (not one): role matrix
    sheds Viewer + CI + Support at the role boundary, AND Support is
    OUTSIDE the cross-tenant exception. A correct CapWrite matrix
    therefore needs TWO regression-prevention pieces compared to a
    CapRead matrix: a deny row for CI / Support at same-tenant via
    ReasonDeniedNoCapability, and an additional Support cross-tenant
    deny row at the engine. Both must be pinned, because either
    half-coverage admits a regression — a catalog change downgrading
    project.update to CapRead would pass a "matrix without the deny
    rows" suite even though it has silently widened the boundary.
  - The project-VIEWER grant on its target project deny is the new
    coverage CapWrite policy matrices need vs CapRead matrices: a
    Viewer grant COVERS the resource but does NOT hold the
    capability, so the engine returns ReasonDeniedNoCapability (not
    ReasonDeniedOutOfScope). A future regression that conflated
    these two reasons (or that widened Viewer's capabilities) would
    fail here. Document this as a CapWrite-policy-matrix template
    addition in Codebase Patterns.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0130
- What was implemented: DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id}, the first
  destructive surface on the project resource. Scheduled (soft) deletion:
  stamps deletion_scheduled_at + audit + bumped version in one tx, leaving
  the destructive teardown (environments/services/audit cascade) for a
  later worker story so the project and its audit trail still exist after
  the response returns.
  - internal/controlplane/store/migrate/migrations/0013_project_deletion_schedule.up.sql
    + .down.sql (new): nullable timestamptz column on projects + partial
    index for the cleanup worker scan. Mirrors migration 0010 for
    organizations one-for-one — same nullability convention (NULL = live),
    same write-once-in-spirit posture, same column-name and index shape.
  - internal/controlplane/store/project.go: new DeletionScheduledAt *time.Time
    field on Project, extended projectColumns + scanProject, and a new
    ScheduleDeletion(ctx, tx, orgID, projectID, ifMatchVersion) method on
    ProjectRepository. The repository keeps the unconditional-UPDATE posture
    deliberately: the customer-facing already-scheduled distinction is the
    service’s job, the repository must remain SQL-idempotent for
    non-customer callers (workers, admin jobs). Stale If-Match goes through
    classifyProjectConcurrencyMiss — the same disambiguation Update
    already uses — so a stale view is reported as ConflictStale with the
    row’s authoritative version, a cross-tenant id stays NotFound.
  - internal/controlplane/store/projectservice.go: new projectDeleteAction
    constant, DeleteProjectInput type (mirrors DeleteOrganizationInput),
    and a new ProjectService.ScheduleDeletion unit-of-work method. The
    composition is: validate (blank orgID/projectID + missing actor org are
    typed errors BEFORE the tx opens), then in Store.Write: Get the current
    row, optionally enforce IfMatchVersion (the version pre-check runs
    BEFORE the already-scheduled check so a stale If-Match wins over an
    already-scheduled message — the same ordering OrganizationService
    uses), reject an already-scheduled row as apierr.Conflict, call the
    repository ScheduleDeletion, record deletion_scheduled_at as audit
    metadata (verbatim RFC3339Nano UTC, non-secret), append the audit
    event. A failure in any step rolls the whole tx back: an audit row
    can never name a deletion that did not change resource state, and a
    second-schedule failure cannot leak a duplicate audit row.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects.go: extended projectResource
    with an optional DeletionScheduledAt *string ',omitempty' field —
    the SAME forward-compatible wire convention organizationResource used.
    Live projects keep the byte-for-byte same wire shape: the field is
    omitted entirely for a NULL stamp. projectResourceOf now projects the
    timestamp. New errNoProjectDeleter sentinel, ProjectDeleter port
    (ScheduleDeletion(ctx, in) (Project, error) — mirroring
    OrganizationDeleter), deleteProjectPayload, and deleteProjectHandler.
    The handler is the same thin shape PATCH uses: principal-from-context
    guard, deleter-nil internal guard, optional If-Match parse (400 on
    malformed), correlation-from-context, delegate to ScheduleDeletion,
    on success ETag header + 202 Accepted envelope (Accepted because the
    destructive teardown is a later worker job, not actually deleted yet).
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/routes.go: registered the new apiRoute
    after PATCH /v1/projects/{project_id}, with RequiresAuth=true,
    RequiredAction=policy.ActionProjectDelete (CapWrite — already in
    the policy catalog at catalog.go:100), resolver=projectIDResolver (so
    cross-tenant project_ids are denied at the policy boundary BEFORE the
    handler runs), SuccessStatus=http.StatusAccepted. Extended
    newRouteTable to accept the new projectDeleter ProjectDeleter param.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/server.go: NewHandler signature gained
    projectDeleter ProjectDeleter (one new positional parameter, slot 30
    in the chain — after projectUpdater, before logger) and the
    newRouteTable call site was updated.
  - cmd/yalla-api/main.go: the existing projectService now also wires the
    new ProjectDeleter slot (the same store.ProjectService satisfies

  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_delete_test.go (new): 9 contract
    tests in package httpapi driving the real NewHandler + real policy
    engine (fake Authenticator + fake ProjectDeleter only) — happy-path

- Learnings for future iterations:
  - The "DELETE on a customer resource" pattern is now stable for the
    second time (organization first, project second): nullable
    deletion_scheduled_at column + partial index, repository
    ScheduleDeletion returns the persisted row, service-layer
    already-scheduled Conflict (the repository stays SQL-idempotent),
    audit metadata captures the resolved stamp time. The next DELETE on
    a customer resource (environments, services) can mechanically copy
    the same six-file shape: migration + struct field + repo method +
    service input/method + httpapi port/handler/route + cmd/yalla-api
    wiring. Returns 202 Accepted because destructive teardown is a
    later worker job.

    resources (organizationResource.DeletionScheduledAt and

    already-scheduled check so a caller with a stale If-Match learns
    "your view is stale" rather than an already-scheduled message that
    might race with a concurrent edit they did not see. Intentional,
    parallels OrganizationService.
  - The bulk substitution `fakeProjectUpdater{}, nil)` ->
    `fakeProjectUpdater{}, fakeProjectDeleter{}, nil)` covered 27/28
    files; the variant `fakeProjectUpdater{}, logger)` in
    me_contract_test.go + server_test.go needed handling separately.
    Workflow for every "add new port to NewHandler" story: (1) define
    new fake in the new contract-test file, (2) python pass over the
    common terminating pattern, (3) grep for residue and fix manually.
    Route-discovery tests using the 27-nil-arg newRouteTable shape need
    exactly one extra nil.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0132
- What was implemented: policy-matrix coverage for DELETE
  /v1/projects/{project_id} — the authorization contract of the
  endpoint BE-0130 wires, parallel to BE-0123 for POST, BE-0126 for
  GET, and BE-0129 for PATCH /v1/projects/{project_id}.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_delete_policy_test.go (new):
    one canonical fixture (canonicalDeleteProject — a project row with
    its deletion_scheduled_at stamp already set, so the wire body on the
    allow path carries the authoritative lifecycle state) + a single
    leak guard (deleteProjectDenyBodyLeak) used by every deny branch,
    then four tests that drive the REAL NewHandler + real
    policy.NewEngine() against fake Authenticator + fake ProjectDeleter
    (the production request path minus the database):
    - TestDeleteProjectPolicyMatrixRoles tables all six built-in roles
      against project.delete at a same-tenant project resource.
      CapWrite splits the matrix: Owner / Admin / Developer allow via
      ReasonAllowedByRole (202 Accepted + deleter reached with home_org
      + path project_id + actor id + actor_org_id + the canonical
      scheduled-deletion row rendered on the wire); Viewer / CI /
      Support deny via ReasonDeniedNoCapability (403 + deleter never
      reached + body never echoes the canonical row). CI denies despite
      holding CapDeploy — CapDeploy is service lifecycle, not
      desired-state mutation. Support denies despite holding the engine
      cross-tenant exception — that exception is gated on (CapRead ||
      CapSupport), so CapWrite is OUTSIDE it even within the home
      tenant.
    - TestDeleteProjectPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys proves a Disabled
      Owner principal (revoked OR expired credential) is denied via
      ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled, the deleter never runs, and the
      body never echoes the principal id, the home org id, or any
      seeded project data. Underlying role is Owner so a working
      credential WOULD allow — Disabled is the only thing in the way.
    - TestDeleteProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal pins the
      cross-tenant boundary at both the wire and the engine. Wire-level:
      an attacker in org_attacker hitting DELETE /v1/projects/{prj_victim}
      surfaces as 404 NotFound at the persistence boundary because
      projectIDResolver builds the resource from the principal's HOME
      org (never the path), so the tenant-scoped repository query runs
      against (org_attacker, prj_victim_alpha) and matches no row; the
      assertions are structural: the deleter is ALWAYS called with the
      attacker's home org id — never with a caller-controlled value —
      and the body never echoes the victim's org id. Engine-level:
      every role (including Support) denies cross-tenant via
      ReasonDeniedCrossTenant, since project.delete is CapWrite and the
      engine clause "CapSupport AND (CapRead OR CapSupport)" does NOT
      admit CapWrite. This is the load-bearing distinction from the
      project.read cross-tenant property: read admits Support
      cross-tenant via ReasonAllowedBySupport, but delete DOES NOT.
    - TestDeleteProjectPolicyGrantContainment is the long containment
      test, parallel to projects_update_policy_test.go: a project-scoped
      Admin grant naming THIS project is allowed at the engine
      (ReasonAllowedByGrant) AND end-to-end at the wire (202 + the
      deleter reached with home_org + path project_id + actor id +
      actor_org_id), then five deny wire tie-ins — a sibling project
      hitting the SAME project-scoped Admin grant, a project-VIEWER
      grant on the target project (covers the resource but holds no
      CapWrite — denied via ReasonDeniedNoCapability, the property a
      "grant role enum re-mapping" regression would catch), an
      environment-scoped grant on the parent project (covers() is
      one-way, denied via ReasonDeniedOutOfScope), a service-scoped
      grant on the parent project, and an organization-level Admin
      grant (allowed via ReasonAllowedByGrant at the engine + 202 at
      the wire). The acceptance criterion "environment-level grants do
      not imply access to production unless production is explicitly
      granted" is doubly enforced: the env-scope grantee can't escalate
      from staging-env to production-env (sibling-env property pinned
      with ActionEnvironmentDelete), and can't escalate from any env to
      the parent project (the shallow-resource property). The
      "service-level grants do not expose parent-level secrets or
      unrelated services" criterion is pinned with three engine
      decisions (sibling-service ServiceUpdate, parent-env EnvWrite,
      parent-project ProjectDelete). An org-level Viewer is the
      load-bearing distinction from the project.read grant matrix —
      allowed for read, denied for delete. The final assertion pins
      the foreign-home-grantee deny: a stolen project-scoped key cannot
      smuggle the grant across tenants because the engine refuses to
      consider the grant when the principal's home org no longer
      matches the grant's scope.
- Files changed:
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_delete_policy_test.go (new)
  - ralph/prd.json (BE-0132 passes:true + notes)
  - ralph/progress.txt (this entry)

  go test ./... (full suite); go test -race ./... (full suite); plus the

  goimports/golangci-lint/staticcheck/govulncheck still not installed locally
  (documented in earlier iterations).
- Results: all my changes pass (-race included). No flaky cross-test fakes —
  this story added a single new test file using only existing fakes
  (fakeProjectDeleter, fakeAuthenticator, orgPrincipal, seedProject,
  deleteProjectHandlerFor, deleteProject, decodeDeleteProject, decodeError).
  No NewHandler/newRouteTable signature change — no call-site churn.
- Remaining risks / follow-ups:
  - The next p=1 pending story is BE-0135 (policy matrix for
    POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/restore). That endpoint is BE-0133
    (still passes:false) — restore depends on a soft-deleted project,
    and the policy boundary requires careful thinking about whether a
    restore can race with a teardown worker (it can't today: teardown
    is not wired). BE-0135 cannot land before BE-0133 because the
    fakeProjectRestorer port doesn't exist yet.
  - The acceptance criterion "Integration tests run against isolated
    Postgres migrations" is N/A for a pure policy-matrix story (no
    persistence path is added here). store/projectservice_test.go
    already covers ScheduleDeletion with Postgres.
  - The acceptance criterion "Secrets, tokens, API keys, cookies, and
    rendered environment variable values are redacted" is N/A for a
    projects row, which stores no secrets. The leak guard covers the
    tenant-identity property (id/slug/display name) instead — the
    relevant invariant for this resource.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - The DELETE policy matrix mirrors PATCH (BE-0129) almost exactly,
    but two assertions changed: (a) the allow-path status is
    http.StatusAccepted (202), not 200, because the destructive teardown
    is scheduled rather than immediate; and (b) the wire body carries
    the canonical project's DeletionScheduledAt stamp, so the allow path
    must also assert env.Data.Project.DeletionScheduledAt != nil. There
    is no request body for DELETE, so the leak guard is one needle
    shorter (no canonical-patch-body field to protect) but the
    canonical-row needles (id, "slug", "display name") still apply.
  - The DeleteProjectInput's ActorOrgID field is part of the audit
    record, NOT just a debug attribute — every allow path must assert
    captured.ActorOrgID == principal home org. This is the same
    contract the BE-0130 contract test pins; carrying it into the
    policy matrix means a future PR that wires a real
    ProjectService.ScheduleDeletion can't accidentally drop the
    actor_org_id without failing here.
  - The "env grant on staging does not imply production access"
    acceptance criterion is best pinned with a SECOND engine decision
    (ActionEnvironmentDelete against the production env scope) inside
    the env-grantee block. Just denying project.delete on the parent
    project would miss the sibling-env property. The pattern: when an
    acceptance criterion has a SIBLING property at the same level as
    the targeted resource, add the sibling deny alongside the parent
    deny in the same block; future grant-engine changes that subtly
    widen one without the other fail here.
  - PATCH's wire tie-ins use only a 200 ok assertion; DELETE's allow
    tie-ins must additionally assert the 202 Accepted status and the
    deletion_scheduled_at field. Forgetting the latter would let a
    handler that silently dropped the scheduled stamp pass the test.

    BE-0132 used.

    contract documents.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Inverse lifecycle endpoints (restore vs schedule-delete) reuse the
    same Repository + Service pattern: the repository is an
    SQL-idempotent UPDATE returning the row (with optional version
    WHERE), and the Service does the lifecycle-state precondition check
    inside the same transaction. For restore: pre-check
    DeletionScheduledAt != nil; for schedule-delete: pre-check
    DeletionScheduledAt == nil. The pre-check is the customer's
    truth-finding step — the repository MUST stay SQL-idempotent so
    workers/admin jobs can retry without surfacing a misleading
    Conflict.
  - When adding a new narrow port that participates in NewHandler's
    arg list, the mechanical churn across NewHandler call sites
    dominates effort. Predictable patterns to script: (a) `<lastArg>,
    nil)` where lastArg is the prior new port, (b) `<lastArg>, logger)`
    for the wired server, (c) `<lastArg>)` for newRouteTable callers
    that omit the logger, (d) `<lastArg>, fakeProjectDeleter{}, nil)` for
    cases where the new port sits between two existing positional
    fakes. A second pass for named-variable arguments (e.g. `updater,
    fakeProjectDeleter{}, nil)`) catches edge cases like the
    projects_update_test helper. The newRouteTable callers with 28 nils
    can be located by counting commas in the call's arg list.
  - For an endpoint whose success status is 200 (the default), the
    OpenAPI route-table contract assertion can match either
    SuccessStatus == 0 (omitted, defaults to 200 in the document) OR
    SuccessStatus == http.StatusOK — only a non-default success status
    (e.g. 201 for Create, 202 for ScheduleDeletion) is asserted
    verbatim. The route description should still spell out 200 OK for
    discoverability.
  - A POST endpoint with an EMPTY request body (like /restore) needs no
    validate.DecodeJSON call — the strict-decode + body-buffering path
    is the cost of having a request body. The handler should still
    forward request correlation IDs and read PathValue from the
    framework router rather than parse the URL.
  - The audit metadata for an inverse-lifecycle endpoint should
    capture the prior state — for restore, that is the cleared
    deletion_scheduled_at stamp read from current.DeletionScheduledAt
    BEFORE the UPDATE — so the audit trail documents what the resource
    looked like before the mutation. Mirroring the schedule-delete's
    metadata.deletion_scheduled_at (which records the new stamp) keeps
    the audit shape symmetric.

## 2026-05-15 - BE-0135
- What was implemented: policy-matrix coverage for POST
  /v1/projects/{project_id}/restore — the authorization contract of the
  endpoint BE-0133 wired, parallel to BE-0132 for DELETE
  /v1/projects/{project_id}. project.restore is CapWrite (same class as
  project.delete), so the role matrix splits identically: Owner / Admin
  / Developer allow via ReasonAllowedByRole, Viewer / CI / Support deny
  via ReasonDeniedNoCapability, and the cross-tenant Support exception
  in the engine (`CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)`) does NOT admit
  CapWrite — so EVERY role, including Support, is denied cross-tenant.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/projects_restore_policy_test.go (new):
    one canonical fixture (canonicalRestoreProject — a project row whose
    deletion_scheduled_at has been CLEARED, the inverse of
    canonicalDeleteProject's set stamp; on the wire body this is the
    authoritative restored lifecycle state) + a single leak guard
    (restoreProjectDenyBodyLeak) used by every deny branch, then four
    tests driving the REAL NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine() against
    fake Authenticator + fake ProjectRestorer:
    - TestRestoreProjectPolicyMatrixRoles tables all six built-in roles
      against project.restore at a same-tenant project resource. The
      allow path asserts 200 OK (the restore is immediate, unlike
      schedule-delete's 202), the restorer was reached with
      (home_org, path project_id, principal id, actor_org_id), the
      canonical restored row rendered on the wire, AND
      DeletionScheduledAt == nil (the inverse of the delete matrix's
      `!= nil` assertion — this is the lifecycle-state property a
      handler regression that rendered a stale, still-scheduled row
      from a store cache would fail). Deny rows assert 403 + the
      restorer never ran + the body never echoes the canonical project.
    - TestRestoreProjectPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys proves a Disabled
      Owner principal (revoked OR expired credential) is denied via
      ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled, the restorer never runs, and the
      body never echoes the principal id, the home org id, or any
      seeded project data. Underlying role is Owner so a working
      credential WOULD allow — Disabled is the only thing in the way.
    - TestRestoreProjectPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal pins the
      cross-tenant boundary at both the wire and the engine. Wire-level:
      an attacker in org_attacker hitting POST
      /v1/projects/{prj_victim}/restore surfaces as 404 NotFound at the
      persistence boundary because projectIDResolver builds the resource
      from the principal's HOME org (never the path), so the
      tenant-scoped repository query runs against
      (org_attacker, prj_victim_alpha) and matches no row; assertions
      are structural — the restorer is ALWAYS called with the
      attacker's home org id, never with a caller-controlled value,
      and the body never echoes the victim's org id. Engine-level:
      every role (including Support) denies cross-tenant via
      ReasonDeniedCrossTenant. Mirror of BE-0132 — restore and delete
      sit on the SAME side of the support cross-tenant exception
      because they're both CapWrite.
    - TestRestoreProjectPolicyGrantContainment is the long containment
      test: a project-scoped Admin grant naming THIS project allowed
      at the engine AND end-to-end at the wire (200 + restorer reached
      with home_org + path project_id + actor id + actor_org_id), then
      five deny wire tie-ins — a sibling project hitting the SAME
      project-scoped Admin grant (ReasonDeniedOutOfScope), a
      project-VIEWER grant on the target project (covers the resource
      but holds no CapWrite — ReasonDeniedNoCapability, the property a
      "grant role enum re-mapping" regression would catch), an
      environment-scoped grant on the parent project (covers() is
      one-way — ReasonDeniedOutOfScope), a service-scoped grant on the
      parent project (and engine-pinned deny on sibling-service
      ServiceUpdate + parent-env EnvWrite to enforce
      "service grant does not expose parent-level secrets or unrelated
      services"), and an organization-level Admin grant (allowed via
      ReasonAllowedByGrant at the engine + 200 at the wire). The
      acceptance criterion "environment-level grants do not imply
      access to production unless production is explicitly granted" is
      doubly enforced: the env-scope grantee can't escalate from
      staging-env to production-env (sibling-env property pinned with
      ActionEnvironmentDelete), and can't escalate from any env to the
      parent project (the shallow-resource property). An org-level
      Viewer is the load-bearing distinction from the project.read
      grant matrix — allowed for read, denied for restore. The final
      assertion pins the foreign-home-grantee deny: a stolen
      project-scoped key cannot smuggle the grant across tenants
      because the engine refuses to consider the grant when the
      principal's home org no longer matches the grant's scope.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The restore policy matrix mirrors the delete matrix almost
    one-to-one: BOTH are CapWrite, BOTH are OUTSIDE the support
    cross-tenant exception, BOTH split the role table identically
    (Owner/Admin/Developer allow, Viewer/CI/Support deny), and BOTH
    are resource-scoped through projectIDResolver so a project-level
    grant CAN authorize them (load-bearing distinction from
    project.create's organization-root resource). The two assertions
    that differ are (a) the allow-path status is 200 (restore is
    immediate) versus 202 (schedule-delete is asynchronous), and
    (b) the canonical row carries DeletionScheduledAt == nil
    (restore cleared it) versus != nil (delete set it). Mirror
    matrices like this are a great pattern: write the inverse-scope
    test by COPYING the existing matrix file and changing the four
    surface bindings (action constant, fake type, store input type,
    decode helper) plus the two assertion differentials above.
  - When the previous iteration ALREADY added a narrow port to
    NewHandler's argument list (BE-0133 added fakeProjectRestorer{}
    to all 32 sibling tests), a follow-up policy-matrix story for the
    SAME endpoint adds zero call-site churn — it reuses the existing
    fakes by simply parameterising over fakeProjectRestorer{project,
    err, got}. Bundling endpoint implementation + matrix into the
    same iteration would have been worse: BE-0133 was already the
    biggest churn-producer in the projects sequence, and dragging
    matrix coverage in would have ballooned its diff further. The
    natural seam is "endpoint + contract tests, then matrix as a
    follow-up" — exactly the BE-0133 -> BE-0135 split here.
  - For an inverse-lifecycle endpoint like restore, the canonical
    fixture's distinguishing property on the wire body is the
    AUTHORITATIVE LIFECYCLE STATE THAT THE OPERATION JUST PRODUCED —
    a cleared stamp for restore, a set stamp for schedule-delete.
    The leak guard's id/slug/display name needles are the same as
    the inverse fixture's (here they differ — prj_restore_alpha vs
    prj_matrix_alpha — only because the BE-0132 matrix used the same
    file in parallel and we want test failure messages to point at
    the right story); the meaningful inversion is asserted in the
    allow-path body decode, not the deny-path leak guard.

    repository methods) intentionally not included; they land with
    BE-0139 (PUT /v1/projects/{project_id}/grants).

    TestProjectGrantRepoListByProjectIsTenantScoped; a full sibling
    test file beside the repository will help when BE-0439's mutation
    methods land.

    TestOrganizationVariableServicePatch*) remain failing on this
